title: The China-Taiwan Diplomatic War Is More About Politics Than Economics
gist: Henry Large traces the PRC-ROC contest for diplomatic recognition since 1949, noting the balance has tilted toward Beijing since UN Resolution 2758; the headline argues it is driven more by politics than economics (truncated excerpt).

insights.claim: Beijing's One China principle forces states to recognize either the PRC or the ROC, not both.
insights.speaker: Henry Large
insights.so_what: Each switch of recognition is a zero-sum political outcome.

insights.claim: Taiwan initially held an advantage in recognition due to US anti-communist messaging and generous economic assistance programs.
insights.speaker: Henry Large
insights.so_what: Historical recognition was shaped by US backing and aid.

insights.claim: After U.N. Resolution 2758 admitted the PRC and expelled the ROC, the contest for international recognition has tilted increasingly in Beijing's favor.
insights.speaker: Henry Large
insights.so_what: Taiwan's diplomatic space has been shrinking; remaining allies are at risk of switching.

insights.claim: The title's claim is that the China-Taiwan diplomatic war is driven more by politics than economics.
insights.speaker: Henry Large
insights.so_what: Economic inducements may not predict recognition switches; watch political triggers.
